The Windows 95 launch was one of the most important events in computer history. If you're not old enough to really remember it, an explanation can't really do it justice. Although computers had been in some folks homes for over a decade, they had only become common in the early 90s. But up until Windows 95 you still had to deal with a command line interface, memory managers, etc. Almost everybody in the US was looking forward to it's release--it was almost like a new Beatles album was getting released. I knew a few folks who actually took off work to stand in line to buy a copy.

I grew up using DOS, and to be quite honest I miss it's simplicity.

The pc didn't lag, typing a command line was often faster than clicking through a cascading menu, you just had to learn them by heart. Games ran fine, your biggest worry was setting up your SoundBlaster settings. System ressources weren't wasted, it wasn't about shiny bells and whistles... holy shit I'm 33 & talk like my grandfather !

I'm a DOS master myself. Those of us who learned it (mostly out of necessity) back in the pre-Windows days generally were ninjas. There was a finite number of commands, and once you learned them you could pretty much do anything. The GUI either just got in the way or removed our ability to do stuff easily. Most folks, however, were just not interested or able to learn a CLI. I remember when most folks who ran Windows 3.1 just had their autoexec's set to load the GUI--they had no idea that it was running on top of DOS 6.2. They'd get themselves into a panic if they accidentally closed Windows and found themselves back in DOS. Win 95 was designed for those folks--which was pretty much 95% of the population. Folks needed a LOT of hand-holding back in the early PC era.

Consider a running DC motor. If the motor is not connected to anything, a fairly constant current flows through it. What happens if you attach a load to it, such as letting it drive a car? Since energy can't be created, it will obviously cause a larger flow of current (assuming the power source is capable).

The same concept applies to the sun, so an increased load (in form of generating electricity) will cause an equal increase in energy drain from the sun. This is still a fairly minor issue though as modern solar panels only have a ~20% efficiency rating. But the energy is produced and flung in all directions regardless of whether or not it's used. If the solar panel wasn't there, the light would hit whatever would have been behind the solar panel.
